title: Voice agents in calls and meetings
subtitle: Speech recognition, synthesis and turn-taking on my own hardware, joined to the platforms people already use

stats.label: faster speech recognition on the GPU than on the CPU path, 18× at the least, in real turns

lede: An AI that people can talk to in a real call has to answer in conversational time, stop when it is interrupted, and keep the audio away from third-party AI services. I built a conversational voice engine in Rust with speech recognition, neural speech synthesis, floor control so several AI voices share one conversation without talking over each other, interruption handling so a person speaking stops the agent, and tool calls made mid-conversation. The gap between the end of a question and the first sound of the reply was taken apart stage by stage. See From two seconds to under one.
quote: A proof that passes with the wrong input is a proof of the test harness.
evidence: Real-time voice AI: a Rust conversational engine on my own GPUs with question-to-first-sound cut from about 2.1 s to about 0.9 s, stage by stage.
Speech recognition and synthesis pipelines: recognition on a GPU at 38 to 74 ms per turn, 18 to 25 times faster than the CPU path, and streaming built for a voice model that had none.
Full-duplex barge-in design: interruptions that only a person can make, with the agent's own echo below a measured threshold and a false stop re-spoken.
Test methodology with negative controls: an echo-cancellation score of 36.8 dB exposed when an unrelated reference scored 37.8 dB, and the proof rebuilt with a control.
Latency diagnosis: a slow Teams turn traced to a shared speech GPU, about 78% of the turn against about 1% for the network, so compute moved and the cloud bridge stayed.
author: Corey James
